newsitem.title: THAILAND: Rumours fly as Thai coalition deadlocked on new PM.
newsitem.headline: Rumours fly as Thai coalition deadlocked on new PM.

text.p: Thailand's outgoing premier and the coalition partners who forced him to quit appeared deadlocked on Tuesday over picking a suitable successor, politicians and analysts said.
They also speculated that if the impasse was not resolved soon, Prime Minister Banharn Silpa-archa might decide to dissolve parliament and call snap elections.

Rumours flew around the Thai stock market late on Tuesday that Banharn was expected to either dissolve parliament or back the appointment of former premier Chatichai Choonhavan as a compromise choice for his successor.
Chatichai heads the opposition Chart Pattana party and was premier during 1988-91, when Thailand's economy boomed, but he was ousted in a military coup in February 1991.
"There was a rumour in the market that Chatichai Choonhavan would join Banharn's coalition and be chosen as the new prime minister," said Songyos Kulvichien of First Asia Securities.
Some television and radio stations also had analysts speculating that Banharn would dissolve parliament later on Wednesday. The rumours could not be verified.
The Thai stock market opened down, but the index closed up 7.84 points, or 0.76 percent, at 1042.21.
Banharn, who agreed last Saturday to quit within seven days after finding a suitable successor, wants to have a big say in the appointment of his replacement, analysts said.
Signs of discord over his successor appeared on Tuesday as a top adviser and elder in Banharn's Chart Thai party, which leads the ruling coalition, declared his right to the top job.
Pramarn Adireksarn, whom Banharn supporters have pushed to succeed him, claimed he was in line for the top post because he was a senior Chart Thai leader and had party support.
His statement frustrated some coalition members who had openly been lobbying for Defence Minister Chavalit Yongchaiyudh, who was behind efforts to oust Banharn, analysts said.
Chavalit leads the New Aspiration Party (NAP), the second largest party in the coalition.

"By tradition and legally, the Chart Thai party has every right and justification to pick one of its leaders to be the new prime minister," Pramarn, 82, told reporters. "I am healthy enough to take up the position.
"Other parties can also nominate their man, but one has to uphold political etiquette," he said.
Chavalit and other ministers attended a regular weekly cabinet meeting on Tuesday that was expected to be the last to be chaired by Banharn.
The premier declined to talk to reporters.
"There is no progress (in seeking a sucessor) at all and I don't want to make any comment to create further confusion of the situation," a bristling Chavalit said before the meeting.
Despite support for Chavalit, a close aide said the chances of his becoming prime minister were slim.
"As Banharn still insists he will propose someone in his party to replace him, the chances of Chavalit becoming premier are less than 40 percent," said the aide, who asked not to be identified.
"I believe that this political standoff will possibly lead to the house dissolution."
Some small coalition parties like the Social Action Party, and the Nam Thai party backed Chavalit for the premiership.

Banharn has kept his silence ever since he was humiliated by his allies on Saturday. They had forced him to declare his resignation in exchange for support in a parliamentary no-confidence motion that Banharn later won.
